best_facts.fact: In Blake's 'London', the third stanza's lines begin How, Every, And, Runs: they spell HEAR, in a stanza about cries no one in power listens to.
best_facts.why_surprising: A hidden acrostic in one of the most taught poems in English.

best_facts.fact: Kafka asked his publisher that the insect in The Metamorphosis not be drawn on the cover, not even from a distance.
best_facts.why_surprising: The most famous bug in literature was never meant to be seen.

best_facts.fact: The earliest author known by name was a woman: Enheduanna, priestess at Ur and daughter of Sargon of Akkad, about 4,300 years ago.
best_facts.why_surprising: Literature's first signature predates Homer by 1,500 years.

best_facts.fact: Akhmatova's Requiem survived Stalin's terror without paper: friends memorised each verse and the scraps were burned.
best_facts.why_surprising: A modern masterpiece transmitted like an oral epic.

best_facts.fact: The CIA secretly printed Doctor Zhivago in Russian in 1958 and handed copies to Soviet visitors at the Brussels World's Fair.
best_facts.why_surprising: A love story used as a Cold War weapon.

best_facts.fact: 'For sale: baby shoes, never worn' is not Hemingway's: similar ads ran in 1906, and the attribution first appears in a 1989 play.
best_facts.why_surprising: Literature's most famous micro-story has the wrong author.

best_facts.fact: The famous 2013 Science study showing literary fiction improves mind-reading failed to replicate in 2016 and 2018.
best_facts.why_surprising: A finding quoted worldwide quietly fell apart.

best_facts.fact: In Yale's long study of 3,635 older Americans, book readers lived about 23 months longer than non-readers.
best_facts.why_surprising: Reading books shows up in mortality statistics.

best_facts.fact: Vedic priests memorised the Rigveda in braided patterns like ghana, running words back and forth, so a single slip would be caught.
best_facts.why_surprising: An error-checking code built from human memory, 3,000 years ago.

best_facts.fact: India was the first country to ban The Satanic Verses, on 5 October 1988, nine days after it was published in Britain.
best_facts.why_surprising: The ban came months before the fatwa.

best_facts.fact: Jane Austen sold the copyright of Pride and Prejudice for £110, and her name was not on the book.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of the best-selling novels ever earned its author a modest one-off fee.

best_facts.fact: Empson wrote most of Seven Types of Ambiguity before he was 22, then was expelled from Cambridge when contraceptives were found in his rooms.
best_facts.why_surprising: A founding text of modern criticism came from a student thrown out of college.

best_facts.fact: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems; fewer than a dozen were published in her lifetime, and her editors replaced her dashes.
best_facts.why_surprising: One of America's greatest poets was almost entirely unpublished.

best_facts.fact: The Great Gatsby sold about 20,000 copies in its first year; Fitzgerald died in 1940 thinking himself a failure.
best_facts.why_surprising: A school-syllabus classic began as a commercial flop.

best_facts.fact: In the Lady Chatterley trial of 1960, the prosecutor asked the jury whether they would want their wives or servants to read the book.
best_facts.why_surprising: One out-of-touch question helped lose the case.

best_facts.fact: Heart Lamp, in 2025, was the first Kannada book and the first short story collection to win the International Booker Prize.
best_facts.why_surprising: Two firsts for one book from Hassan, Karnataka.

best_facts.fact: Flaubert tested his sentences by shouting them in a room he called his gueuloir, his shouting room.
best_facts.why_surprising: The master of the exact word worked by ear, at full volume.

side_dish.title: Sherlock Holmes, the detective who read people like poems
side_dish.body_md:
Arthur Conan Doyle trained as a doctor in Edinburgh under the surgeon **Joseph Bell**, who liked to astonish students by telling a stranger's job and travels from his hands, posture and tan before the patient spoke. Doyle built Sherlock Holmes on that habit. In *A Study in Scarlet* (1887), Holmes's first words to Watson are a deduction: 'You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.'

Holmes's method is close reading applied to the world. He notices the small, overlooked detail (a worn cuff, mud of a certain colour, a dog that did not bark in the night), treats it as evidence, builds a claim and tests it against the rest. In 'A Scandal in Bohemia' (1891) he scolds Watson, who has climbed the stairs at Baker Street hundreds of times without knowing there are 17 steps: 'You see, but you do not observe.' Richards' students, Nabokov's exam questions and Holmes's stairs are the same lesson.

The parallel runs both ways. Crime fiction trains readers to notice clues, just as Chekhov's gun trains them to watch details. Literary critics borrowed the word 'clue' for the hints that unlock a text, and the historian Carlo Ginzburg argued in 1979 that detectives, doctors and art experts share one 'evidential paradigm', reasoning from small traces to hidden causes.

offline_task.title: Close-read Blake's 'London' with a pencil
offline_task.body_md: Print or copy out William Blake's 'London' (16 lines, free on Project Gutenberg). Read it aloud once, quickly. Then read it slowly with a pencil: circle every repeated word ('every', 'charter'd', 'marks'), underline sounds you hear, and mark where the poem turns. Check the first letters of the third stanza. Finally, write one sentence that makes a claim about the poem, and copy two phrases that prove it. Keep the page: it is the first entry in your commonplace book.
